content: 1. Although kanamycin (KAN) is no longer recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) for the treatment of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB), it is included in this analysis for historical context. Additionally, mutations associated with KAN resistance provide valuable insights into interpreting certain mutations that confer resistance to amikacin (AMK). 2. WHO has not yet established a critical concentration (CC) for pretomanid (PMD). However, this second edition offers preliminary guidance for interpreting loss-of-function (LoF) mutations in six genes required for the activation of this prodrug. 3. Guidance is also provided for rifapentine (RPT), with specific recommendations for its interpretation. 4. This report on the second edition of the mutation catalog describes revisions to the methods used to create the catalog, identifies mutations, and summarizes key findings for each drug. It also outlines new areas for future research. 5. The catalog aims to support the development of new and improved molecular assays, based on sequencing or other methods, for the comprehensive detection of resistance to tuberculosis (TB) drugs. 6. The second edition of the catalog consists of three related elements: A list of graded variants, including a master file and a file with genomic coordinates in VCF format. Evidence-based additional grading rules, which are either general or drug-specific. Evidence-based other interpretation criteria. 7. These elements can be used to interpret Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) mutations detected through next-generation sequencing (NGS) or other genotypic drug susceptibility testing (gDST) methods. 8. The catalog includes specific examples of how mutations are graded and interpreted. For instance: Mutations in the katG gene, such as Ser315Thr and Ser315Ile, are graded as Group 1 and Group 2 mutations, respectively, and are interpreted as markers of isoniazid (INH) resistance. Loss-of-function mutations in katG, such as Gly33fs, are classified as Group 2 mutations and are considered to confer high-level INH resistance. Silent mutations, such as the G>A mutation at position 1350 of rpoB, are classified as Group 4 mutations according to general grading rules. 9. The second edition includes significant updates over the first edition, such as: An expanded list of target genes associated with resistance to all drugs considered. Inclusion of mutations conferring resistance to bedaquiline (BDQ) and linezolid (LZD), identified through laboratory-based selection experiments. 10. A total of 52,567 isolates were analyzed in the second edition, up from approximately 38,000 in the first edition. Data were contributed by 67 countries, with substantial increases in isolates resistant to most drugs, except ethionamide (ETO). 11. The catalog evaluates the performance of mutations in predicting phenotypic resistance by calculating sensitivity, specificity, and positive predictive value (PPV). However, these metrics are influenced by factors such as the prevalence of resistance in different settings and the quality of phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (pDST) data. 12. The catalog emphasizes the importance of understanding local epidemiology when using WHO-endorsed gDST assays. The pre-test probability of resistance to second-line drugs is a critical factor in interpreting results. 13. The second edition includes >5,800 new isolates with BDQ pDST and nearly 7,000 new isolates with LZD pDST. These additions enhance the analysis of genotypic-phenotypic associations for new and repurposed drugs. 14. The catalog groups mutations into five categories based on the strength of evidence supporting their association with drug resistance. These groups are used to guide the interpretation of mutations and their clinical significance. 15. The catalog also highlights the need for independent validation of results using different datasets to better understand the performance of mutations, particularly rare ones, in predicting resistance. 16. The second edition provides detailed instructions for interpreting mutation tables, including terms, abbreviations, and color coding to indicate confidence grading criteria. This explanation provides a clear and detailed understanding of the content, suitable for a professional audience.
